text:
As Panagbenga Festival paints Baguio City in full bloom, expect vibrant parades, heavier traffic, and thousands of happy festival goers filling the streets. 🌼✨

Here’s your quick guide before heading out:

🚧 Road Closures
Major roads like Session Road, Harrison Road, and Magsaysay Road will have early morning closures during parade days. Plan ahead and leave early.

🚶 Best Way Around the CBD
Once you’re in the city center, walking is your best friend. Wear comfy shoes, stay hydrated, and enjoy the street energy.

🧭 Pro Tip for Foodies
When the crowd gets overwhelming and your feet need a break, step away from the noise and recharge with a feast that’s just as festive.

At Myeongdong Jjigae, the flavors are blooming too. 🌸🔥 From unlimited samgyup (with unlimited cheese!) to comforting buffet options or hotpot, it’s the perfect pause between parades. Refuel, cool down, and get back to the celebration energized.

📍 2F City Hub, 92 Gen. Luna Rd (Corner Leonard Wood), Baguio City
🕥 10:30 AM – 9:00 PM

Celebrate the colors outside. Taste the bloom inside.
See you at Myeongdong Jjigae. 💛

text:
The Panagbenga Festival, also known as the Baguio Flower Festival, is a month-long annual celebration held every February in Baguio City, Philippines. The term "Panagbenga" comes from a Kankanaey term meaning "season of blooming" or "a time for flowering."
 
The festival was conceptualized in 1995 to honor Baguio City's flowers and as a way to help the city recover from the devastation of the 1990 Luzon earthquake. It has since become a vibrant display of the rich cultural heritage of the Cordillera region, showcasing various events, exhibitions, and activities that promote the history, traditions, and values of Baguio and the Cordilleras.

As part of the celebration of the 30th Panagbenga Festival, 25 Cordilleran ethnic groups showcased the culture, traditions and the katarakian of the highlanders during the Rhythm of the Highlands: A Showcase of Culture and Dance. Featuring ritual, victory, courtship, occupational and festival dances, the event was held at the Melvin Jones Grandstand, Baguio City on February 15, 2026.

Participating groups included:
1. e-BICAS Cultural Group
2. SAKUSAK Musical Ensemble
3. GASAT SIN DAP-AY Cultural Dance Group
4. SAGANDAYAN Cultural Group
5. CHAG-AY Cultural Ensemble
6. KASIYANA YA BALINTAUGAN
7. IYAMAN Cultural Group
8. GANNAY Cultural Dance Troupe
9. DANG - DANG AY Cultural Group
10. BUMADANG Cultural Group
11. GAWIS Culture and Arts Ensemble
12. SALAKNIB Youth Ensemble
13. ISEM - Cordillera Dance and Culture Advocates
14. UGGAYAM Cultural Dancers
15. RAGSAK Cultural Group
16. Saint Louis School of Pacdal Inc. IP Socio - Cultural Dance Troupe
17. GAMENG DI CORDILLERA
18. KAYAW DI UMILI Ensemble
19. LITAGWA Cultural Preservation Group (LCPG)
20. KAFAGWAY Cultural Group
21. SALIBI Cultural Group
22. BSU KONTAD - Highland Cultural Dance Troupe
23. GARDENERS’ Tribe Cultural
24. AMBARU Cultural Group
25. TURAYAN Cultural Group

text:
The Panagbenga Season of Blooming: A Story of Spirits, Sun, and Survival 🌸✨

Reimagined video by: Grand Revel Creatives | Earl Haro

Music arranged by: @cs.musicalproductions (TikTok) | "Dong Dong Ay" by ALAMAT

Panagbenga is more than just a festival; it is the heartbeat of the Cordilleras. Long before the first float moved down Session Road, the indigenous tribes believed these mountains were the Land of the Anito. Every wildflower was seen as a gift from the spirits, and a bountiful bloom was a divine sign of favor for the fertility of the earth.
In those early days, wild sunflowers—associated with the Sun God looking down on the peaks—signaled the start of the dry season, a time for the community to gather in celebration.

But the most powerful "folklore" is Baguio’s own rebirth. Following the devastating 7.7 magnitude earthquake in July 1990, the city stood in ruins. From that despair, a vision of hope emerged. In 1995, Panagbenga was born—a metaphorical "blooming" from the rubble, proving that like a flower breaking through the frost, Baguio could rise again.

Today, the rhythm of the Bendiyan Dance echoes this journey. Once an ancient Ibaloi war dance for victory in battle, it has been reinterpreted into a dance of unity—a celebration of our collective victory over hardship.

From the ancient spirits to the modern streets, we dance, we bloom, and we remember. 🥁🌻🏙️

🌸 Did You Know? 🎶

The Panagbenga Hymn was originally composed on February 8, 1989 by Professor Macario “Mac” Fronda, a longtime music educator and bandleader from Saint Louis University who helped shape Baguio’s musical culture.

Although it became the official song of the Panagbenga Festival, the hymn was first written to inspire athletes in the Palarong Pambansa before being adopted for the festival.

Professor Fronda passed away on March 14, 2013, at the age of 91 due to complications from prostate cancer, and the Panagbenga Hymn remains one of his most beloved legacies.

Today, it continues to be sung as a symbol of unity, hope, and the ever-blooming spirit of Baguio City. 🌼✨

text:
The official music of Panagbenga, commonly known as the Panagbenga Hymn, emerged during the festival’s early years in the mid-1990s, when organizers sought a unifying piece that would capture Baguio’s recovery, resilience, and renewed spirit after the 1990 earthquake. The hymn was composed by the late Dean Macario “Mac” Fronda Jr. of the Saint Louis University (SLU) Band. 

Drawing from Baguio’s cultural pride and close ties to nature, the hymn was written with a celebratory yet solemn tone suited for parades and mass performances. Through the years, while arrangements have been adapted for different ensembles and generations, the original composition remains intact. Today, the Panagbenga official music continues to be a defining sound of the festival—symbolizing unity, gratitude, and the enduring spirit of Baguio every blooming season.

text:
CAN I INTERVIEW YOU IN JAPANESE? 🎤🇯🇵

ネパール出身の男性3人組、渋谷に現る 🇳🇵🔥
3 men from Nepal appear in Shibuya 🇳🇵🔥

🇳🇵🤝🇯🇵🔥

渋谷のど真ん中で出会った、ネパール出身の男性たち。
In the middle of Shibuya, I met these men from Nepal.

「どこから来ましたか？」
“Where are you from?”

「ネパールです」
“From Nepal.”

3人ともネパール出身。
All three are from Nepal.

今は日本で働いている。
Now they’re working in Japan.

「何の仕事をしていますか？」
“What do you do?”

「レストランです」
“I work at a restaurant.”

「コンビニです」
“At a convenience store.”

それぞれの場所で、
At different places,

日本語を使って働いている。
they’re using Japanese to work.

「アルバイト？」
“Part-time?”

「はい、バイトです」
“Yeah, part-time.”

慣れない環境でも、
Even in an unfamiliar environment,

しっかり前に進んでいる。
they’re moving forward.

そして——
And then—

「日本語の早口言葉できる？」
“Can you do a Japanese tongue twister?”

「生麦 生米 生卵」
“Namamugi, namagome, namatamago”

「ガス バス カパス」
“Gas, bas, kapas”

笑いながらも挑戦する姿。
Trying while laughing.

最後はネパール語の早口言葉。
And finally, a Nepali tongue twister.

言葉を超えて、
Beyond language,

ちゃんと伝わるものがある。
something still connects.

あなたは早口言葉、得意ですか？ 🤔
Are you good at tongue twisters? 🤔

「日本語が上手」とは、完璧に話すことではなく、
こうして勇気を出して日本語で話してくれる人たちのことです。

Being “good at Japanese” isn’t about perfection —
it’s about having the courage to speak like this.
